chunks: My father (RA) said: Sa'd ibn Abd Allah said: Abu al-Khayr Saliḥ ibn Abu Hammad said: Abu Khalid al-Sijistani related to me, on the authority of Ali ibn Yaqtin, on the authority of Abu Ibrahim (AS), who said:

The Commander of the Faithful (AS) passed by a group in Kufah while they were arguing about the Divine Decree. He asked their speaker: 'Are you able to act because of Allah, with Allah, or without Allah?' The person did not know how to answer. So the Commander of the Faithful (AS) said: 'If you claim that you are able to act because of Allah, then you are not in trouble. However, if you claim that you are able to act with Allah, then you have claimed to be an associate with Him in His sovereignty. And if you claim that you are able to act without Him, then you have testified to a god other than Allah, the Mighty and High.' He replied, 'No, O Commander of the Faithful! I am able to act because of Allah.' So the Imam (AS) said: 'If you had said something else, I would have hit your neck.'
ai.seo_question: What is the Shia theological understanding of human capability in relation to Divine Decree according to Imam Ali?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *al-Tawhid* illustrates the Shia doctrine of *Amr bayn al-Amrayn* (a position between absolute determinism and total free will) through Imam Ali’s rhetorical trilemma on human capability (*istita'ah*). By rejecting 'with Allah' as *shirk* (partnership) and 'without Allah' as independent divinity, the Imam affirms that human power is contingent upon Allah’s will yet distinct enough to warrant accountability, a nuance that distinguishes Shia theology from the Mu'tazila and Ash'ari schools.
